[0day] [exploit] Advancing exploitation: a scriptless 0day exploit against Linux desktops

What I really like about this exploit is that it shows that there's a variety of weaknesses in a classic location: file parsing and display.

The proliferation of formats (and the expectation that they function natively) has yielded a variety of potential vectors of attack on the "unified desktop" use case (the most common use case for computers, but not as absolutely ubiquitous as in prior years, where you generally use one reasonably powerful computer for all computing tasks).

The take home message to open source devs is nothing new: code needs to be audited and reviewed, boundaries need to be checked, etc. They already know this- there's just more functionality across the world of computing than there is time to audit it to a high degree.

The take home message to users is generally also nothing new: you need a general idea of which data can be a "basilisk", killing you when you look at it, and generally everything excepting text is at least a little vulnerable to this, with the rarer and more complex formats more of a potential risk.

The good news out of this exploit is interesting: the authors selected Fedora as their test case because it uses all the protection measures, and as such is a good test case. The side effect of this is that customizing this exploit to every desktop may not be possible: each distribution would have a different attack vector. That itself is a step forward from "breaks any machine with the exploitable code on it". It's probable that a full recompile with different optimizations could give you some resistance, etc. The general effect of stuff like randomizing address space etc. should be to increase the complexity of an attack and reduce the valid targets a given exploit should hit, so that part is at least encouraging.

Overall, it is an excellent reminder that the more tasks a computer is expected to be able to follow, the more vulnerable code exists on that machine.
